docs.title: Connectors: import and sync
docs.text:
Tasks can come from other platforms as well as from harnesses. There are two features, and you can use either alone:

  • aiculator import loads items once, each time you run it.
  • The synchronizer keeps them in step afterwards, in both directions.
Source kind Import Status back Changes in Live changes Jira Cloud jira JQL Yes Polling Webhook Notion notion Filter Yes Polling Webhook Excel .xlsx xlsx Whole sheet or regions No Re-reads the file No CSV csv Whole file No Re-reads the file No

Tested against documented behaviour, not live accounts

The Jira and Notion connectors are tested against local servers written from each vendor's API documentation, and .xlsx against files written by openpyxl. They have not yet run against a real Jira site, a real Notion workspace or a file saved by Excel. Start with aiculator source check and --dry-run.

docs.title: Configure a source
docs.text:
Sources live in .agents/sources.yaml, which is safe to commit because it holds no secrets. Credentials are named by environment variable, and the file is refused if it contains a value instead.

JiraNotionEisenhower tableEisenhower grid 
sources:
  - name: jira
    kind: jira
    url: https://acme.atlassian.net
    auth: {email_env: JIRA_EMAIL, token_env: JIRA_TOKEN}
    query: project = PROJ AND status = "Ready for agent"
    fields:
      title: summary
      spec: description
      priority:
        from: priority.name
        map: {Highest: 100, High: 50, Medium: 10, Low: 1}
      labels:
        team: customfield_10010
      props:
        story_points: customfield_10016
    defaults:
      tier: 1
      checks: ["go test ./..."]
      require_review: true
      aging: [1h=5, 4h=20]

sources:
  - name: roadmap
    kind: notion
    data_source: 1f2e3d4c-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
    auth: {token_env: NOTION_TOKEN}
    filter:
      property: Status
      status: {equals: Ready}
    fetch_body: true          # Costs one more request per page
    fields:
      title: Name
      spec: body
      status: Status
      tags: Skills
      priority:
        from: Priority
        map: {P0: 100, P1: 50, P2: 10}

One row per task, with a column for each axis.

sources:
  - name: matrix
    kind: xlsx
    path: eisenhower.xlsx
    sheet: Tasks
    fields:
      key: ID
      title: Task
      spec: Notes
      priority:
        rules:
          - when: {Urgent: "yes", Important: "yes"}
            value: 100
          - when: {Important: "yes"}
            value: 50
          - when: {Urgent: "yes"}
            value: 25
        default: 1
      labels:
        quadrant:
          rules:
            - when: {Urgent: "yes", Important: "yes"}
              value: do
            - when: {Important: "yes"}
              value: schedule
            - when: {Urgent: "yes"}
              value: delegate
          default: delete
      props:
        due: Due

One column per quadrant, with regions saying which cells are which.

sources:
  - name: grid
    kind: xlsx
    path: matrix.xlsx
    regions:
      - {name: do, range: "A3:A40"}
      - {name: schedule, range: "B3:B40"}
      - {name: delegate, range: "C3:C40"}
      - {name: delete, range: "D3:D40"}
    fields:
      title: value
      priority:
        from: region
        map: {do: 100, schedule: 50, delegate: 25, delete: 1}
      labels:
        quadrant: region

docs.title: Field mapping
docs.text:
Field Sets title The task's title. Required spec Its instructions priority, tier Numbers tags Required capability tags labels Named labels props Named properties key What identifies a row in a file. Without it, the title does status Which field holds the status, when it isn't the system's own

Each can be a field name, or an object with from, map, rules and default. Names ignore case, and priority.name follows a nested field. Rules run in order, and the first whose when matches gives the value.

skip_when leaves items out, such as skip_when: [{Status: Done}].

Outside data cannot choose what runs

checks, touches, budget, require_review and allow_empty can only come from defaults, in this reviewed file. No mapping can set them, because checks are commands the swarm runs, and anyone who can edit a ticket would otherwise be able to choose them. A config that tries is refused. spec/alloy/swarm.als models this rule, and a test ties that model to the code.

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
aiculator source check jira            # Are the settings and credentials right?
aiculator import jira --dry-run        # What would happen? Changes nothing
aiculator import jira
aiculator import jira --query 'key = PROJ-1'
aiculator import jira --update         # Bring earlier imports up to date

A task's ID comes from the item's key, such as jira-PROJ-123, so importing again is safe. Items already imported are left alone, and --update changes only what they say, never their progress.

Jira attachments and Notion files become foreign resources, which are only downloaded when asked for. See Labels, priority and attachments.

Dependencies come across too. In Jira, a Blocks link makes the blocked issue wait, and tasks are created in dependency order. A cycle is reported and left out. If an item is blocked by something the import did not include, the task comes in without that dependency, because it would otherwise wait forever. The import warns you, and the task's unresolved_deps property records it.

Export your credentials before aiculator up

The import reads credentials from your shell. The synchronizer and attachment downloads run in the server, which reads them from the environment it was started in.

docs.title: Sync
docs.text:
Add a sync section, and the server keeps that source in step:

    sync:
      direction: both                # both, push or pull
      push:
        mode: realtime               # realtime, or interval with every: 1m
        updates: partial             # partial sends each change, last sends only the end
      pull:
        mode: interval               # once, interval or webhook
        every: 5m
      create: false                  # Also create tasks for new items
      status:                        # Which remote status each state becomes
        claimed: In Progress
        running: In Progress
        review: In Review
        done: Done
        canceled: Cancelled
      on_remote:                     # What a remote status does here
        Cancelled: cancel

A state left out of status is not sent.

You want Set Status on the other side within milliseconds push.mode: realtime Fewer calls, sent in batches push.mode: interval, with every Only the final result push.updates: last Each change along the way push.updates: partial One read when the server starts pull.mode: once A read every so often pull.mode: interval, with every Changes as they happen pull.mode: webhook

Check how it's going:

aiculator sync status

docs.title: Who wins
docs.text:
Each side owns different things, so there is nothing to merge:

What Owner Title, description, labels and priority The other system How far along a task is The swarm Stopping a task Either, through on_remote

If someone moves a remote status to something not listed in on_remote, the swarm doesn't fight them, and its next state change sets the status again. The only action is cancel, because a remote status must not be able to mark work as done without verification.

Before each push the swarm reads the item, so that it doesn't overwrite a cancel it hasn't seen yet. A very small window remains between that read and the write.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
Webhooks need the server to be reachable from the internet, and it listens on 127.0.0.1 by default, so you need a tunnel or a reverse proxy in front of it. The address is POST /v1/hooks/SOURCE.

Every delivery must carry a valid signature, checked against the raw bytes before anything in it is believed. A delivery only says which item changed, and the swarm then reads that item once. A read also runs at each start, which catches what was missed.

JiraNotion

Register the webhook with a secret, and set the same secret here:

sync:
  hook_secret_env: JIRA_HOOK_SECRET
  pull: {mode: webhook}
  1. Set hook_secret_env, but leave the variable unset for now.
  2. Create the subscription in Notion. It sends a one-time token to the server.
  3. Read it with aiculator sync hook-token SOURCE, and paste it into Notion's form.
  4. Set the variable to that token, and restart the server.

docs.title: How sync stays out of the way
docs.text:
The synchronizer is a side effect. It reads the commit stream through a durable consumer, on its own goroutines, after each commit.

  • A slow or dead remote can't slow a claim. Tests stop the remote entirely and measure claims.
  • Nothing is lost. A change that wasn't sent is delivered again after a restart, soon after a crash and at once after a clean stop.
  • Bursts cost one call. Newer changes replace older ones that haven't been sent, so the last state wins.
  • Changes don't echo. The link records the last status either side saw, and a status the remote already has is never sent.
  • Rate limits are respected. Retry-After is honoured, pushes run four at a time, and failures back off for up to 5 minutes.
  • One bad source stays contained. A source with missing credentials shows up in sync status, and the rest carry on.

spec/tla/Sync.tla checks that sync always settles, that the two sides agree once it has, that a cancel the swarm has seen stops the task, and that no change echoes, including across crashes.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:
On an Apple Silicon laptop, with the remote's own time left out:

Measure Result Commit to remote call, realtime p50 2.4 ms, p99 3.5 ms Claim p50, without and with sync 20 µs and 27 µs Import About 10,000 tasks per second Claim p99 during an import, with 20,000 tasks waiting 1.3 ms

internal/connect/perf_test.go and internal/swarm/perf_test.go hold these to a budget.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Comments aren't synced. Only status goes back.
  • A deleted item isn't noticed. Its task carries on.
  • A Notion-hosted file's link expires after about an hour. Fetch it soon after importing, or import again with --update.
  • Spreadsheets are read-only, and an .xlsx formula gives its last saved result.
  • Sync settings load at start. Restart the server after changing them.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text:
There are two live views of the same data: aiculator top in a terminal, and aiculator web in a browser. Both are read-only.

Many projects?

aiculator top --all and aiculator web --all show every project on this machine. See Realms.

docs.title: Terminal
docs.text:
aiculator top
Key Action 1 to 5, or tab Switch between overview, tasks, sessions, flow and usage ↑ ↓, or j k Scroll r Live mode on or off: redraws four times a second, so a change shows as it happens. --live starts in it p Pause q Quit

The overview has a table per tier: ready, working, in review, parked, failed and done, with the agents at that tier and how many are waiting. A tier with ready work and no agent is marked !, because nothing will pick that work up. The tasks view shows each lease and progress deadline next to their lengths (lease ttl 2m00s, progress ttl 10m00s). The sessions view shows each connected agent: how it connects, its harness, its state, any usage limit, its wait hold, and the host, process, parent and folder it runs in.

Golden files in internal/tui/testdata/golden hold every screen after each step of a scripted swarm on a fake clock. A change to any screen shows in the test; go test ./internal/tui -run Golden -update accepts it.

Without a terminal, it prints one frame and exits, so it works in scripts:

aiculator top --once --view usage
aiculator top --json | jq '.usage.tokens'

--no-color and NO_COLOR turn color off. Status is always in words as well as color.

docs.title: Web
docs.text:
aiculator web             # Opens your browser
aiculator web --no-open   # Prints the link
aiculator web --ttl 1h    # Expires sooner; the default is 12 hours

It follows your system's light or dark setting, works at phone width, and pauses while its tab is hidden.

docs.title: Sessions and controls
docs.text:
A table lists the connected sessions, the same as aiculator sessions: kind (acp for aiculator drive, mcp for the stdio bridge, mcp-http for a harness talking MCP directly, shell for aiculator work), harness and model, state, task, when it was last seen, how long it has been connected, its wait hold, and where it runs. A session that goes quiet shows as gone, and leaves the list after five minutes.

aiculator web --control opens a link whose page also has three buttons:

  • Remove disconnected clears the gone sessions now.
  • Stop all agents tells every agent to exit. Each gets exit from its next wait, or from the wait it is in, and what it holds goes back to the queue with no penalty.
  • Kill agent processes also ends the processes aiculator started for agents on the server's machine, such as aiculator drive and the harness it runs. It checks that each process id still runs aiculator first. A harness you started yourself is only told to exit.

A control link can do these and read the dashboard, and nothing else. The same is on the command line: aiculator sessions forget, aiculator agents stop --all, aiculator agents kill --all, with --realms for every project.

docs.title: Flow analytics
docs.text:
Below the live numbers, four charts show how work has flowed. Filter them by time window (the last hour up to everything kept), by tier and by label. On aiculator web --all, a realm filter picks the project.

  • States: a Sankey of the path each task took, Draft → Ready → Claimed → Running → Review → Merging → Done, and where it left that path for Failed, Parked or Canceled. A node bigger than what leaves it holds tasks that are still there. A task that failed and then made it counts once, on the path it finished; its retries are in the funnel.
  • Why tasks fall out: each time a task failed or was parked in the window: the state it was in, then the reason. Reasons are the swarm's codes, such as no_progress, checks_failed, review_rejected, budget_exhausted, needs_resplit, unreadable_record and done_without_verification. A note an agent wrote when it gave up shows as agent_note, so that its text never becomes a chart label.
  • Tries: how many tasks reached a first, second or third try, and how many finished on each one.
  • What caused retries: what ended the try before each new one. A failure's reason counts first. Otherwise it's the last reason the task had, such as an expired claim.
  • Cumulative flow: how many tasks were in each state over time, stacked with done at the bottom. A band that keeps growing, such as review, is a bottleneck.

The charts come from the event log, which keeps every committed change, so a restart loses nothing. The server reads the log into a compact index when it starts, then follows it. Until it has caught up, the card says so. Tier and label filters use each task's tier and labels now. Working out the charts for 20,000 tasks takes about 9 ms.

The dashboard is a plugin compiled into the binary. go build -tags noweb leaves it out, saving about 0.1 MiB.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text: How many tasks are in each state, and how often tasks have moved between states. Many running → failed moves mean agents are struggling, and merging → failed means merge conflicts.

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text: Rates over the last minute, with per-second history for the last 60 seconds.

docs.title: Latency and jitter
docs.text:
Row Measures What a high value means Queue wait From ready to granted Not enough agents Commit One durable write The disk or the store is struggling API call One call, leaving out long-polls The server is struggling. progress and submit are slower by nature, because they save work with git. Task cycle From created to merged Tasks are slow or retrying

Jitter is how much consecutive samples differ, smoothed the way RFC 3550 does for network jitter. High jitter with a low median points to occasional stalls.

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
Each task holding a lease is one of:

Health Meaning OK Plenty of time left At risk Under a quarter of its lease or progress time remains Expired Past its deadline, and about to be taken back

"Progress left" counts down until the agent must change files. An agent that heartbeats without changing anything runs out of this and is caught as a zombie. Problems sort to the top, and the list holds at most 200 tasks.

Agents are working, waiting, idle or gone, which means not seen for 30 seconds.

docs.title: Probes
docs.text: Probe Checks writer The engine answers store The state store answers event_log The event log is keeping up git The repository and integration branch are readable sandbox Which sandbox checks run in

docs.title: Usage and budgets
docs.text:
Tokens come from harnesses that report them over ACP, or from --tokens and the tokens tool argument. Cost is only what agents report, in micro-dollars, because the swarm does not know your prices. It reads zero when nothing reports it.

Totals by task and tier come from durable state, so they survive a restart. Rates and per-agent figures start again when the server restarts.

docs.title: For other tools
docs.text:
Endpoint Token Use GET /v1/healthz None Is the process up GET /v1/readyz None Is it ready. Returns 503 if a probe fails, with no details. GET /metrics Viewer Prometheus format GET /v1/observe Viewer The full snapshot as JSON GET /v1/sessions Viewer Connected sessions as JSON GET /v1/events Viewer Every change as JSON lines, each with a seq. ?since=SEQ or Last-Event-ID resumes after it, so delivery is at least once; a {"gap": true} line says older events are gone GET /v1/analytics Viewer The flow analytics as JSON. Takes window (such as 6h, 7d or all), tier, label (key=value or key) and points GET /v1/events Viewer Every task change, as JSON lines

Create a read-only token for a scraper with the API's /v1/tokens route, setting viewer: true. aiculator web --no-open also prints one in its link.

aiculator events | jq -r 'select(.state == "parked") | "\(.id): \(.reason)"'

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Viewer tokens can read but cannot add tasks, take work or mint tokens.
  • The page and its scripts hold no data, so they need no token. All data does.
  • The link's token sits in the URL fragment, which browsers never send to a server. The page then removes it from the address bar and keeps it only for that tab.
  • A strict content security policy blocks anything from elsewhere and anything inline.
  • Task titles and agent names come from agents, so they are untrusted. The web page only ever renders them as text, and the terminal view strips control characters so they cannot steer your terminal.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
Aiculator's logging works like Kubernetes: -v=0 to -v=9, with --vmodule to raise one component on its own. If you know kubectl -v=8, you already know how to use this.

aiculator task ls -v=6                  # See the HTTP calls this command makes
aiculator up --v=4                      # Start a server with debug logging
aiculator debug verbosity 5 --for 10m   # Trace a running server for ten minutes
aiculator logs -f --component engine    # Follow what it is doing

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
The levels mean what kubectl's mean. aiculator debug levels prints this list.

Level kubectl's meaning What it shows here 0 Always visible to an operator Errors, and verbosity changes 1 A reasonable default Server start, serious warnings such as a lost planner or a stale revision 2 Steady state; recommended A server's default. Task transitions, plans, MCP tool calls, sessions, merges 3 Changes in detail Every commit and grant, rejected commands and why, permission decisions, checks starting 4 Debug Why an agent was told to wait or exit, worktrees, check output, sandbox commands 5 Trace Every git command, why a task was not eligible, compare-and-swap revisions 6 Requested resources Method, URL, status and time of each HTTP call 7 HTTP headers Also headers, with credentials removed 8 HTTP contents Also bodies, MCP arguments and agent text, cut to 1 KiB, with credentials removed 9 HTTP contents, untruncated Also bodies up to 1 MiB, with credentials removed

A command defaults to 0 and a server to 2. Precedence is the flag, then AICULATOR_V, then the default. All these forms work: -v=6, -v 6, --v=6 and --v 6.

Logs go to stderr, so stdout stays clean for scripts, even at level 9.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
At level 5 on a server, one task being granted:

level=INFO msg="task created" v=2 component=engine task=fix-login title="Fix the login redirect" tier=1 plan_epoch=0
level=INFO msg=commit v=3 component=engine task=fix-login kind=publish actor=system:plan took=65.542µs
level=INFO msg=compare-and-swap v=5 component=engine task=fix-login from_rev=1 to_rev=2 lease=0
level=INFO msg="task transition" v=2 component=engine task=fix-login from=draft to=ready tier=1 attempt=0 actor=system:plan reason=""
level=INFO msg=commit v=3 component=engine task=fix-login kind=grant actor=worker1 took=59.333µs
level=INFO msg=compare-and-swap v=5 component=engine task=fix-login from_rev=2 to_rev=3 lease=1
level=INFO msg="task transition" v=2 component=engine task=fix-login from=ready to=claimed tier=1 attempt=1 actor=worker1 reason=""

At level 6 on a command:

level=INFO msg=request v=6 component=client method=GET url=http://127.0.0.1:7777/v1/tasks status=200 took=752.833µs bytes=412

At level 8, asking for a token. The caller gets the token on stdout, and the log shows none of it:

level=INFO msg="request headers" v=7 component=client method=POST path=/v1/tokens headers="Authorization: [redacted]; Content-Type: application/json"
level=INFO msg="request body" v=8 component=client method=POST path=/v1/tokens body="{\"agent\":\"demo\",\"tier\":1}"
level=INFO msg=request v=6 component=client method=POST url=http://127.0.0.1:7777/v1/tokens status=200 took=736.75µs bytes=134
level=INFO msg="response headers" v=7 component=client path=/v1/tokens headers="Content-Length: 134; Content-Type: application/json; Date: ..."
level=INFO msg="response body" v=8 component=client path=/v1/tokens status=200 body="{\"token\":\"[redacted]\"}"

docs.title: One component at a time
docs.text:
Raising everything to 5 is noisy. --vmodule sets a level per component, can use wildcards, and can also lower one:

aiculator up --vmodule engine=5,work=4
aiculator up --v=5 --vmodule http=0

The components are engine, work, driver, swarm, sandbox, mcp, http, client and store.

docs.title: On a running server
docs.text:
No restart is needed, and anything in progress carries on:

aiculator debug verbosity                        # Show the current setting
aiculator debug verbosity 5 --for 10m            # Trace, then go back by itself
aiculator debug verbosity --vmodule engine=5 --for 5m
aiculator debug verbosity 2                      # Change it for good

Use --for. It means a debugging session cannot leave a server logging heavily because someone forgot. Changing the level needs the admin token, and the change itself is logged.

docs.title: Reading the logs
docs.text:
aiculator logs reads the log of a server started with aiculator up:

aiculator logs --tail 50
aiculator logs -f --component engine
aiculator logs -f --grep fix-login

For other tools, --log-format json writes one JSON object per line, and --log-file PATH writes to a file:

aiculator logs -f | grep 'task transition'
aiculator up --log-format json --v=3

aiculator top never writes logs to the screen, because they would corrupt it. Use --log-file to capture them.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: Question Try Why does this task never start? aiculator debug verbosity --vmodule engine=5 --for 2m, then look for not eligible. It names the tier, tags and file conflict. Why does this agent keep waiting? At level 4, wait answered gives the action and reason Why was a command refused? At level 3, command rejected gives the state and reason Why did the checks fail? At level 4, check output holds what the command printed What is git doing? At level 5, git lists each command and how long it took Why was a tool call denied? At level 3 on the driver, permission decision gives the tool and kind What is this client sending? -v=8 on the command

docs.title: What is safe to share
docs.text:
Credentials are removed where lines are written, so no call site can leak one by mistake. Tests read the logs at level 9 on both the client and the server, after real calls over HTTP and MCP, and fail if a token appears. Anything named like a credential is removed, as is anything shaped like a token or a bearer header, wherever it appears.

Levels 8 and 9 show content

Task titles, specs, notes and agent messages all appear. Credentials are removed, but your code and instructions may be in there, so read a level 8 or 9 log before sharing it.

The log file is not rotated

.swarm/server.log grows as long as the server runs. Level 9 fills it quickly, which is another reason to use --for.

A disabled log call costs about 2 ns and allocates nothing, so debug logging can stay in the hottest paths.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
aiculator export writes tasks and other data to a file. You choose what goes in, and the format.

aiculator export                       # All tasks, as JSON
aiculator export -o tasks.xlsx         # The file name picks the format
aiculator export --format html -o report.html
Format Use --format Or a file ending in JSON, the default json .json YAML yaml .yaml, .yml CSV csv .csv Tab-separated tsv .tsv Excel xlsx .xlsx An HTML table html .html, .htm A Markdown table md .md

docs.title: What to export
docs.text:
Tasks are the default. You can also export agents, usage, flow or realms:

aiculator export realms --format md
aiculator export agents -o agents.csv

JSON and YAML keep the whole record, and the table formats start with the most useful columns. To choose your own, use --fields. Dots reach inside, and --list-fields shows what exists:

aiculator export --list-fields
aiculator export --fields id,title,labels.team,owner -o tasks.csv
aiculator export --with-meta --fields id,meta.story_points -o points.xlsx

--with-meta adds each task's properties as meta.NAME. It costs one request per task.

docs.title: Which rows
docs.text:
aiculator export --state running,review
aiculator export --label team=core
aiculator export --where tier=2
aiculator export --sort -priority --limit 10

docs.title: Across projects
docs.text:
--all includes tasks from every running realm, with a realm column. --realm NAME exports just one, from any folder:

aiculator export --all -o everything.xlsx
aiculator --realm shop export -o shop.csv

docs.title: Opening an export safely
docs.text:
Task titles and specs can come from agents, or from tickets anyone could edit, and an export often gets opened somewhere that acts on what it reads. So every value is treated as text:

Format What protects you CSV, TSV A value a spreadsheet would run as a formula, such as =HYPERLINK(...), starts with a ' Excel Every text cell is stored as a string, never as a formula HTML Every value is escaped, and the page's policy stops anything in it from running Markdown Values can't end their cell or form links or tags

That leading ' means a CSV value can differ slightly from the original. For an exact copy of the data, use JSON or YAML.

An empty field shows as blank. A task's record leaves out values that are zero, so a priority of 0 is blank too.

docs.title: Join from an open harness
docs.text: You can turn a harness session into a swarm worker at any time, including one that was open before the swarm existed.

docs.title: Set up once per project
docs.text:
aiculator join --tier 1

Name harnesses with --harness claude,opencode. Without it, every harness found on your PATH is set up. To allow planning as well, add --planner.

docs.title: Choose a route
docs.text:
Route Needs a restart? Works for How Shell No Any harness that can run commands Paste the line below MCP Yes, MCP loads at session start Harnesses with a project MCP file Use the swarm-join skill

The line to paste into a session that is already open:

Read .agents/skills/swarm-join/SKILL.md and follow it.

The skill checks whether the session has the swarm's tools. If it does not, it uses aiculator work commands instead. Pi and goose always use this route.

docs.title: Choose a tier
docs.text:
The tier says what work a session takes: 1 standard, 2 advanced, 3 ultra.

  • Manual: give it with the skill, such as /swarm-join 2, or in the line you paste ("Join as tier 2").
  • Asked: with no tier given, the skill asks which one. Press Enter for auto.
  • Auto: the swarm picks from the model and the effort or variant it runs at. The model's family sets the tier: Haiku, mini and flash models are 1; Sonnet, GPT-5, o3, GLM and Qwen Coder are 2; Opus, Fable, the pro models and Gemini Pro are 3. High, max or ultrathink effort moves it up one, and low or minimal moves it down one. So does a thinking budget of 16,000 tokens or more, or under 2,000. An unknown model gets tier 1, since taking easy work costs less than failing hard work.
aiculator work join --tier auto --model claude-sonnet-5-5 --effort high
# joined at tier 3 (ultra): auto: claude-sonnet-5-5 is a tier 2 model, high effort moves it to 3

The skill passes the model and effort it knows it runs as. What it leaves out comes from the harness's environment: AICULATOR_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_MODEL, OPENAI_MODEL and the like, and AICULATOR_EFFORT, CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, OPENAI_REASONING_EFFORT or MAX_THINKING_TOKENS. On the MCP route the skill calls join_swarm with the same choices; it is refused while the session holds a task.

docs.title: What a joined session can do
docs.text:
Both routes offer the same operations:

Operation MCP tool Shell command Get the next task wait_for_task aiculator work wait Take a specific task claim aiculator work claim Extend the lease heartbeat aiculator work heartbeat Save work progress aiculator work progress Finish submit aiculator work submit Give up fail aiculator work fail Hand back with no penalty release aiculator work release Review another agent's work review_verdict aiculator work verdict See the swarm situation aiculator work situation Report usage report_usage, or tokens and cost on most calls aiculator work usage, or --tokens and --cost Say the harness ran out report_limit aiculator work limit Estimate a task's tokens estimate_tokens aiculator work estimate Choose the tier join_swarm aiculator work join --tier

A session joined with --planner also gets plan_begin, plan_update, plan_add and plan_commit. See Plan work.

docs.title: What the answers mean
docs.text:
Each wait returns an action:

  • task: you hold a lease on that task, and workdir is where to do it.
  • wait: nothing yet, and reason says why: planning, planner_lost, deps, tier_busy or idle.
  • exit: stop. No more work can reach this tier, an operator stopped the session (stopped_by_operator), or it reported a usage limit (usage_limit, with when it resets).

docs.title: Waits that cost fewer tokens
docs.text: Each wait is a model turn, so a wait should be held as long as the harness lets a call run. Harnesses rarely document that limit, so the swarm learns it per session. A wait that ran to the end makes the next one 5 seconds longer, up to 40. A caller that hung up early marks where its limit is, and later waits stay 3 seconds under it. So leave hold_seconds and --hold unset. next_hold_seconds in each answer, and the HOLD column in aiculator sessions, show where a session has got to.

docs.title: Usage and limits
docs.text:
Report tokens and cost whenever the harness says what a turn cost, so budgets, the dashboards and estimates stay right. If the plan's usage, credit or rate limit runs out, report it with when it resets. What the session holds goes back with no penalty, and its waits answer exit until then, so it stops spending turns.

A joined session is not sandboxed

It runs under your harness's own permissions. In one test, a model started its own server in a temp directory on its own initiative. The acceptance checks still run in the sandbox, but for work you do not fully trust, use sandboxed workers.

OpenCode 2

A running OpenCode background service does not pick up new project config, and opencode mcp list shows the service's view. Use opencode run --standalone or restart the service. The shell route works either way.

docs.title: Undo
docs.text:
aiculator unjoin

This removes the swarm's MCP entries and skill links, and nothing else. Add --purge to delete the swarm's skills from .agents/skills too.

docs.title: MCP config
docs.text: aiculator join sets up MCP for you. These commands give you direct control, for one harness or any config file.

docs.title: Add
docs.text:
aiculator mcp add                               # Every installed harness
aiculator mcp add --harness opencode --tier 2   # By id
aiculator mcp add --harness claude,cursor --global
aiculator mcp add --harness ~/.local/bin/opencode   # Found from its executable
aiculator mcp add --harness ./custom/mcp.json   # A config file; format inferred
aiculator mcp add --harness opencode --dry-run  # Show it; change nothing

--harness accepts auto, all, harness ids, a path to a harness's executable, or a path to a config file. For a config file, the format comes from its name: .toml means Codex's format, opencode* means OpenCode's, and anything else is the common mcpServers JSON. Override it with --format.

docs.title: Print the config piece
docs.text:
To add it by hand, print it. This changes nothing.

$ aiculator mcp print --harness opencode
# opencode: add to opencode.json
{
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "swarm": {
        "command": [
          "aiculator",
          "mcp",
          "--auto",
          "--tier",
          "1",
          "--harness",
          "opencode"
        ],
        "timeout": {
          "execution": 60000
        },
        "type": "local"
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Any other server
docs.text:
These commands manage any MCP server, not only the swarm's. Give it a name and put its command after --:

aiculator mcp add --name docs --harness claude -- npx -y docs-server
aiculator mcp print --name docs --harness codex -- npx -y docs-server
aiculator mcp add --name api --env API_URL=https://x --harness cursor -- api-server

--env values are stored in plain text

Do not put real secrets in a file you commit.

docs.title: Remove
docs.text:
aiculator mcp remove --harness opencode                # The swarm's entry
aiculator mcp remove --harness opencode --name docs    # A named one

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• The swarm's entry holds no token. The bridge, aiculator mcp --auto, gets its own when it starts, so these files are safe to commit.
  • Your other settings stay. Each change is merged, and the previous file is saved in .swarm/backups/.
  • A file it cannot understand is left alone. That includes invalid JSON and opencode.jsonc, which may hold comments. You get the piece to paste instead.
  • Timeouts are set for you. The wait_for_task call can hold for up to 40 seconds, so the entry allows 60.

docs.title: Parallel subagents in one worktree
docs.text:
The swarm keeps work apart at three levels:

Level Keeps apart How Realm Projects Separate servers and stores Worktree Tasks Separate checkouts, reviewed and merged one by one Wave Subagents within one task The same checkout, with claims that cannot overlap

Worktrees are the stronger separation, and the right choice for separate tasks. A wave is for one piece of work that splits into parts, where a merge would be overhead. There is no merge step to catch a collision, so aiculator parallel is deliberately cautious.

flowchart TD
    A["List jobs and the files each will change"] --> B["aiculator parallel plan"]
    B --> C{"Verdict"}
    C -- Sequential --> D["Do them one at a time"]
    C -- Parallel --> E["aiculator parallel snapshot"]
    E --> F["One subagent per job in the wave"]
    F --> G["aiculator parallel verify"]
    G -- "Only claimed files changed" --> H{"More waves?"}
    G -- "Unclaimed files changed" --> I["Stop and look"]
    H -- Yes --> E
    H -- No --> J["Done"]

docs.title: Use it from a session
docs.text:
aiculator init installs the swarm-parallel skill, which walks a model through all of this. To change how it behaves, use the parallel-subagents template or the <ParallelWork> component instead:

aiculator template --install parallel-subagents --set max=3

<ParallelWork max="3" title="Split the build" />

docs.title: Use it by hand
docs.text:
# jobs.yaml
jobs:
  - id: api
    touches: [internal/api/users.go, internal/api/users_test.go]
  - id: db
    touches: [internal/db/users.go]
  - id: docs
    touches: [docs/users.md]
    reads: [internal/api/users.go]
  - id: format
    exclusive: true
    deps: [api, db, docs]

$ aiculator parallel plan --file jobs.yaml -o plan.json
Parallel: 4 jobs in 3 waves, compared at dir level.
  Wave 1: api, db
  Wave 2: docs
  Wave 3: format
Field Meaning touches What the job writes: a file, or a directory ending in / reads What it relies on staying the same while it works. A write conflicts with this, and two reads don't deps Jobs that must finish in an earlier wave exclusive Runs alone, as for a formatter or a dependency install weight Rough size. Jobs with the longest chain after them go first

A job with no touches runs alone, because nothing says where it will write. Run the wave with one subagent per job, and check it afterwards:

SNAP=$(aiculator parallel snapshot)        # Before the wave. Stages and commits nothing.
aiculator parallel verify --plan plan.json --wave 1 --since "$SNAP"

verify exits with 1 if a file changed that no job in the wave claimed. It also lists jobs that changed nothing, which can mean a subagent didn't do its work.

docs.title: Granularity
docs.text:
Level Two jobs conflict if they share Use repo Anything Everything runs one at a time dir A directory The safest level that still allows parallel work file A file Most work symbol A symbol or line range in a file Only when you ask for it auto, the default The coarser of dir and file that loses no parallelism

Sharing one file is opt-in, on purpose

With --granularity symbol, file#Charge and file#Refund can share a wave, as can file:1-10 and file:20-30. auto never does this. When we tested this on a real model and asked it to split one file, it made up symbols to fit, and the two subagents collided. So auto treats those claims as the whole file, and at symbol level a claim must exist: a symbol must appear in the file, and a line range must fit. That catches invented claims, but it can't keep a subagent inside its part.

docs.title: How the schedule is worked out
docs.text:
The planner builds a graph with an edge between any two jobs that conflict, and then fills waves, respecting deps and --max.

  • Up to 14 jobs: an exact search over which jobs are finished, which finds the fewest possible waves. A test checks it against trying every assignment.
  • More than that: a greedy schedule that puts the longest chains and most contested jobs first. It says if it can't prove the result is the shortest.

The same input always gives the same plan.

docs.title: What this does and doesn't guarantee
docs.text:
Guaranteed by tests on random job sets: no two conflicting jobs share a wave, every job runs exactly once, and nothing starts before what it depends on.

These limits remain:

  • It relies on the job list being honest. A job that writes a file it didn't list isn't prevented from doing so. verify catches that afterwards, if no other job in the wave claimed the file.
  • verify works per file. It can't tell which job in a wave changed a file, and it doesn't see files ignored by git.
  • Subagents are told, not forced, to keep to their files. A sandbox per subagent would enforce it, and that's what worktrees are for.

docs.title: How well this works
docs.text:
scripts/gate_ui_templates.sh tests this on a real Claude Code session, using Haiku:

Probe Result on the real model Three jobs on three files Planned, ran three subagents in one turn, and verified Two jobs on one file Told Sequential, and made both edits itself, one at a time

Other harnesses have not been tested this way.

docs.title: Plan work
docs.text: A plan turns a spec into many tasks, and keeps waiting workers informed while that happens. The swarm-plan skill walks a model through it, or you can drive it by hand.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
# 1. Take the lease BEFORE reading the spec. Workers now wait instead of exiting.
aiculator plan begin --ttl 5m          # Prints the epoch

# 2. Renew it as you go, and tell workers what you are doing.
aiculator plan update --epoch 1 --ttl 5m --phase "reading code"

# 3. Publish what is coming.
aiculator plan update --epoch 1 --ttl 5m --phase splitting --expected 1=12 --expected 2=3

# 4. Add tasks. Workers cannot see them yet.
aiculator plan add --epoch 1 --id api --title "Add the API" --tier 2 --check "go test ./api"
aiculator plan add --epoch 1 --id ui --title "Add the UI" --dep api --check "npm test"

# 5. Publish the whole plan at once.
aiculator plan commit --epoch 1

docs.title: What workers see
docs.text:
{
  "action": "wait",
  "reason": "planning",
  "planning": {
    "epoch": 1,
    "phase": "splitting",
    "expected_tasks": {"1": 12, "2": 3},
    "age_ms": 180,
    "stale": false
  }
}

docs.title: Rules the swarm enforces
docs.text:
• A hint is a promise. Agents may exit once nothing is expected at or below their tier. After that, the swarm refuses tasks and hint changes that would have reached them.
  • One planner at a time. A second one is refused while the lease is live.
  • A crashed planner cannot do damage. If the lease expires, its drafts are canceled, the epoch rises, and its old epoch is refused. Waiting workers see planner_lost.
  • A plan cannot deadlock. Commit rejects dependency cycles and unknown dependencies.

docs.title: Writing good tasks
docs.text:
• Start low on the tier. Failures escalate automatically.
  • Always give a --check that fails before the work and passes after it.
  • Declare --touches path, so that overlapping tasks do not run at the same time.
  • Keep tasks small, because a worker sees only its own spec and the code.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
There are three ways to extend Aiculator, depending on how much you need.

Way Needs a rebuild? Can do Use it for Event stream No Read every task change Notifications, logs, in any language Program on PATH No Add a command Your own tools Compiled in Yes Add commands, server routes and event handlers Features that ship inside the binary

docs.title: List what you have
docs.text:
$ aiculator plugin
NAME     KIND         DESCRIPTION
webdash  compiled in  Web dashboard, embedded in the binary

docs.title: Event stream
docs.text:
aiculator events | while read -r line; do
  echo "$line" | jq -r 'select(.state == "done") | .id' | xargs -I{} notify-send "Done: {}"
done

docs.title: A program on PATH
docs.text:
Any executable named aiculator-NAME runs as aiculator NAME, the way git does it. It receives AICULATOR_DATA and AICULATOR_VERSION.

#!/bin/sh
# Save as aiculator-greet, somewhere on your PATH.
echo "Hello from $AICULATOR_VERSION"

Built-in commands always win, so a program cannot replace one. Only PATH is searched, so cloning a repository cannot add a command.

docs.title: A compiled-in plugin
docs.text:
Plugins compile in because Go's dynamic plugin package needs cgo, and this binary is static.

A plugin registers itself and implements up to two interfaces:

examples/plugins/hello/hello.go
package hello

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "sync/atomic"

    "github.com/spf13/cobra"

    "github.com/Grano22/aiculator/pkg/plugin"
)

type Plugin struct{}

func init() { plugin.Register(Plugin{}) }

func (Plugin) Name() string        { return "hello" }
func (Plugin) Description() string { return "Example plugin that counts finished tasks" }

// Setup runs once in the server.
func (Plugin) Setup(h *plugin.Host) error {
    var done atomic.Int64
    h.OnEvent(func(e plugin.Event) {
        if e.State == "done" {
            done.Add(1)
        }
    })
    h.HandleViewer("count", http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, _ *http.Request) {
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "%d\n", done.Load())
    }))
    return nil
}

// Commands is optional, and adds CLI commands.
func (Plugin) Commands(cli *plugin.CLI) []*cobra.Command {
    return []*cobra.Command{{
        Use:   "hello",
        Short: "Say how many tasks are done",
        RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, _ []string) error {
            s, err := cli.Snapshot(cmd.Context())
            if err != nil {
                return err
            }
            fmt.Printf("Hello. %d tasks are done.\n", s.States["done"])
            return nil
        },
    }}
}

Include it with a small file in cmd/aiculator, in your own fork:

cmd/aiculator/plugins_hello.go
//go:build example_hello

package main

import _ "github.com/Grano22/aiculator/examples/plugins/hello"

Then build with its tag:

go build -tags example_hello ./cmd/aiculator

Leave out the build tag line if it should always be included. The web dashboard works the opposite way: it is in by default, and -tags noweb removes it.

docs.title: What a plugin can do
docs.text: Method Purpose h.Handle(path, handler) A route with no token, for what anyone on this machine may read, such as static files h.HandleViewer(path, handler) A route that needs a viewer or admin token h.OnEvent(fn) Be told about every task change h.Snapshot(ctx) Read the live dashboard data h.Log Log with the plugin's name attached Commands(cli) Add CLI commands, and use cli.Snapshot and cli.ViewerToken

docs.title: What the swarm guarantees
docs.text:
• A plugin cannot take the server down. One that fails or panics in setup is disabled alone, and a panic in a handler fails only that request or event.
  • A slow plugin cannot slow the swarm. Events are dropped for it rather than waited on, so delivery is best effort.
  • Routes stay in their own space, under /plugins/NAME/, so a plugin cannot shadow the API or another plugin.
  • A command cannot replace a built-in. It is skipped, with a warning.

Compiled-in plugins are fully trusted

A plugin is ordinary Go code in your process, and these guarantees are about mistakes, not malice. Read a plugin before you build it in.

pkg/plugin and pkg/observe are the public API. They may still change before version 1.0.

docs.title: Realms: many projects on one machine
docs.text:
A realm is one project with its own server and its own store. A project becomes a realm when its server starts, and is named after its folder.

aiculator realm ls                     # Every project, and which are running
aiculator top --all                    # All of them, live in the terminal
aiculator web --all                    # All of them, in the browser
aiculator --realm shop task ls         # Act on one from any folder
aiculator realm rename billing-api billing
aiculator realm forget old-project     # Takes it off the list; its data stays

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
aiculator top --all has three views, which you switch with 1 to 3 or Tab:

View Shows Realms Each project: running or not, tasks ready, being worked on, in review, done and parked, and agents working Tasks Tasks in progress or needing attention, with their project and owner Agents Each agent, with its project and current task

Use --once to print one frame, --view tasks to choose the view, and --json for the raw data.

aiculator web --all shows the same in a browser, and each running realm links to its own full dashboard. It runs for as long as the command does, on 127.0.0.1, behind a token in the link it prints.

A single project's aiculator top also names its realm.

docs.title: How projects stay apart
docs.text:
Realms are not merged into one server. That would make one crash, or one damaged store, every project's problem.

What could go wrong What stops it A repository inside another uses the outer one's server The search for a project's data stops at the edge of the repository A stray ~/.swarm claims every folder below it The search also stops at your home directory After a crash, a project's old address now reaches another project's server Each server says which it is, and the client checks That old port is still taken when the project restarts The server picks a free port instead of failing A token from one project is used on another Each project signs with its own key, so it is refused Two servers start on one project The data directory is locked Servers starting together damage the list of realms Each realm is its own file, written atomically A stuck server freezes the view of the others Each is read separately, with a 2-second limit

The list in ~/.aiculator/realms holds names and paths and no tokens. Sandboxed checks can't read it.

docs.title: Agents and realms
docs.text:
A session belongs to the realm of the folder it started in, and can't see the others. Every task it gets says which project the work belongs to, in realm and realm_path. A session that started in the wrong place can notice that.

To pin a session to one project wherever it starts, add --realm to its MCP command:

aiculator --realm shop mcp --auto --tier 1

docs.title: Letting a session move between projects
docs.text:
This is off by default, because it gives a session work in folders you may not have opened it for. To allow it, add --realm-switch to the MCP command:

aiculator mcp --auto --tier 1 --realm-switch

The session then has two more tools: realm_list and realm_use. realm_use is refused while the session holds a task, because a lease belongs to one realm. It has to submit, fail or release the task first.

A joined session runs under its harness's permissions

Moving to a realm doesn't change what the session may do, or where its harness lets it write. Check that its permissions cover the other project before you allow this.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The views read, and don't change anything. To act on a realm, use --realm NAME.
  • The tasks view shows work in progress and work needing attention. Queued and finished tasks are counted in the realms view.
  • One machine only. The list is local, and remote servers aren't included.
  • Totals reset per project. Rates are per server, so there is no combined history across restarts.
  • realm_list shows a project as running if it has an address file, which can be out of date after a crash. aiculator realm ls checks properly.

docs.title: Recovery and failover
docs.text: The swarm keeps one writer per project and checks its own records each time it starts. This page covers what happens after a crash, how to check a project's health, and how to keep a second server ready to take over.

docs.title: Damaged records are repaired at startup
docs.text:
When the server starts, it checks every task record before accepting work. Two kinds of damage are fixed:

  • A record that can't be read. The original bytes go to quarantine. In its place is a parked task titled Unreadable record, kept in quarantine, so that the problem shows up in aiculator top and isn't silently dropped.
  • A record that breaks a rule. For example, a task that is claimed without a lease, or in review with nobody who submitted it. It is moved to the nearest safe state, usually back to Ready. A task marked Done without an independent check is never left as Done. It is parked so that a person decides. The original record is kept in quarantine before it is changed.

Repairs never lower a task's lease number, so a worker holding an old lease can't write over the repaired record.

docs.title: aiculator doctor
docs.text:
aiculator doctor          # report; exits non-zero if something is wrong
aiculator doctor --fix    # also fix what can be fixed safely
aiculator doctor --json

With the server running, doctor reports:

  • records repaired at the last start, and what is in quarantine
  • leases more than a minute overdue (zombie workers)
  • worktrees whose task is gone, done or canceled
  • how far the event log lags behind the store
  • how many tasks are parked

--fix removes the orphan worktrees. With the server stopped, doctor still checks the files in .swarm: a stale pid, an addr that points at nothing or at another project's server, and whether the lock is free. --fix removes the stale files but never the data.

docs.title: Backups of chosen tasks
docs.text:
Some tasks matter more than others. Rules in .agents/backups.yaml keep copies of the tasks they match, outside the store, as plain files:

dir: /Volumes/backup/aiculator   # default .swarm/backups; another disk is better
rules:
  - name: critical
    match:
      labels: {severity: critical}   # a value is a glob: "*" means any value
    journal: true                    # a copy each time one changes
    keep: 50                         # per task
    meta: true                       # also keep its metadata
  - name: releases
    match:
      ids: ["release-*", "hotfix-*"]
      states: [review, merging, done]
    every: 1h                        # a snapshot of all of them, every hour
    keep: 48
    keep_for: 7d
  - name: everything
    match: {all: true}
    every: 1d
    keep: 14

A rule matches a task when every field it sets matches. Within a list, any entry may match. The fields are all, ids (globs), labels, tags, states and min_priority.

  • The journal keeps a copy each time a matching task changes in a way that matters. A heartbeat that only moves a deadline isn't copied. It follows the store's commit stream, so it never slows a claim or a commit, and it catches up on restart: a copy that wasn't written before a crash is written after it.
  • Snapshots keep every matching task at one moment, in one compressed file. One is taken when the server starts if the last one is older than every.
  • Retention: keep copies are kept per task (journal) or per rule (snapshots), and keep_for removes older ones. The newest copy is always kept.

Every file is written under a temporary name and renamed, so a crash leaves a whole file or none.

aiculator backup status                 # what each rule has kept, and any error
aiculator backup now [RULE]             # take a snapshot now
aiculator backup versions TASK          # every kept copy of a task
aiculator backup restore TASK           # newest copy that differs from the task now
aiculator backup restore TASK --before 2h
aiculator backup restore --from FILE --all --dry-run

A copy is history, not a command, so a restore makes it safe first:

  • Work that was in flight in the copy goes back to Ready.
  • The lease number moves on, so an agent still holding the old lease can't write.
  • A Done copy without an independent check is parked.
  • The record being replaced goes to quarantine, so a restore can be undone too.

A restore puts back the task record only. Metadata kept with meta: true is in the copy for reference.

docs.title: A standby server
docs.text:
aiculator up --standby

This starts the server if it isn't running, and then a second one that waits. If the first one stops or dies, the standby takes over on the same address, normally within a second, and open sessions reconnect to it. Leases survive the switch: no lease expires in the first seconds after a takeover (--restart-grace), so workers have time to reconnect.

aiculator down stops the standby first and then the leader, so a clean stop doesn't hand over. /v1/healthz reports a term that goes up by one each time a server becomes leader, so a client can tell that a takeover happened.

docs.title: Why the lock decides who leads
docs.text:
The leader is whichever server holds the lock on .swarm, not whichever one answers health checks. A leader can pause without dying: a stopped terminal, a debugger, heavy swapping or a slow disk. A paused leader doesn't answer, so a standby that took over on a missed health check would be writing while the old leader still believes it leads. When the old leader wakes, there are two writers. The kernel only frees the lock when the process has exited, so with the lock that can't happen.

spec/tla/Election.tla models both versions. The lock version keeps at most one writer and always ends up with a leader. The health-check version (ElectionBug_health.cfg) fails in five steps: lead, pause, take over, wake, two writers.

One machine only

Both servers must run on the same machine against a local directory. File locks on network filesystems such as NFS or SMB aren't reliable enough to decide who writes.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Skills live in one place, .agents/skills/, the cross-client convention from agentskills.io. Harnesses that scan it need nothing, and the rest get a symlink, so an edit reaches all of them.

.agents, plural

Harnesses scan .agents/skills, so that is the main location. Skills in .agent/skills are picked up too, and linked across.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
aiculator skill --install '*'                   # All skills, to every installed harness
aiculator skill --install 'swarm-*' '*-tool'    # By pattern
aiculator skill --install '*' --global          # ~/.agents/skills and home directories
aiculator skill --install '*' --harness all     # Every supported harness
aiculator skill --install x --harness claude,pi
aiculator skill --install x --path ./vendor/skills --harness none
aiculator skill --install x --source ~/my-skills
aiculator skill --install x --copy              # Copy, for tools that do not follow links

Patterns use * for anything, ? for one character and [abc] for a set.

Quote your patterns

A bare * works: the shell expands it into the directory listing, and aiculator recognizes that exact list as "all". But zsh stops with an error on an unmatched *-sth before aiculator runs, so quote anything else.

docs.title: Manage
docs.text:
aiculator skill --list                # Versions, lint state and who can see what
aiculator skill --lint                # Check against the Agent Skills spec
aiculator skill --new my-skill --description "..."
aiculator skill --uninstall 'swarm-*'           # Remove links; keep the source
aiculator skill --uninstall 'swarm-*' --purge   # Also delete the source

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Your own directories are never replaced, even with --force.
  • A skill that fails the linter is not linked anywhere.
  • Reinstalling keeps your edits to a bundled skill. --force restores the bundled version.

docs.title: Bundled skills
docs.text: Skill Use swarm-join Work the queue. It only starts when you ask for it. swarm-plan Turn a spec into tasks. swarm-parallel Split one task among subagents in one worktree, without conflicts. swarm-operate Start the server, add tasks, launch workers.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Use the spec's fields first. These are understood everywhere:

---
name: my-skill              # Must match the directory
description: What it does and when to use it, in words people actually use.
license: MIT
compatibility: Requires git and internet access.
allowed-tools: Read Bash(git:*)
metadata:                   # String values only, so quote numbers
  version: "1.0.0"
---

Some fields work only in certain harnesses. Others ignore them, so they are safe in project skills, but claude.ai uploads and the Skills API reject them.

Field or file Honored by disable-model-invocation Claude Code, Cursor, Pi paths Claude Code, Cursor when_to_use, argument-hint, arguments, user-invocable, disallowed-tools, model, effort, context, agent, hooks Claude Code icon, color Cursor agents/openai.yaml Codex

aiculator skill --lint explains each of these when it finds one.

docs.title: Labels, priority and attachments
docs.text:
A task can carry more than a title and a spec. These features are kept apart from the task's working state, so adding data never slows a claim.

You want Use Where it lives A small fact to filter or sort by A label On the task record, up to 64 labels of 256 bytes each Priority that rises with waiting Aging steps On the task record, or the server's flags Structured or larger data A property The metadata store, up to 256 KiB per task A file A blob The blob store, up to 64 MiB each Something that lives elsewhere A foreign resource A reference, fetched once when asked for

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
aiculator task add --title "Fix login" --label team=core --label sprint=42
aiculator task amend ID --label sprint=43 --label team=

name= removes a label. amend also changes the title, spec, priority and aging, and never touches a task's progress: an agent working on it keeps its lease.

docs.title: Priority that rises with waiting
docs.text:
Every waiting task already gains one priority point per minute, which you can change with --aging-unit. This keeps low-priority work from waiting forever.

Aging steps add jumps at chosen times, so that a task overtakes others once it has waited long enough:

aiculator up --aging 1h=5,4h=20                          # Every task
aiculator task add --title "Report" --aging 30m=50       # This task, replacing the server's steps
aiculator task priority ID                               # How its priority is worked out now

The highest step reached counts, and steps do not add up: 1h=5,4h=20 means +5 after an hour and +20, not +25, after four.

Nothing is rewritten as tasks wait. The boost comes from the task's steps and the time it became ready, so a restart rebuilds the same queue. Each boost costs one heap move, so a claim stays as fast with aging on as with it off. A test checks the order against a brute-force sort of every waiting task.

When a task goes back to ready, because it failed or was released, its wait starts again.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
aiculator task prop ID points=5 team=core 'tags=["a","b"]'
aiculator task prop ID points=     # Removes it
aiculator task meta ID

Values that parse as JSON keep their type. Two writers changing different properties cannot undo each other.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
aiculator task attach ID design.pdf
aiculator task fetch ID design.pdf -o copy.pdf

A blob is named by the hash of its contents, so storing a file twice costs nothing.

docs.title: Foreign resources
docs.text:
A foreign resource refers to something elsewhere, such as an HTTP link or a Jira attachment. Nothing is downloaded until someone asks for it. The bytes are then kept as a blob, so the other system is contacted only once.

aiculator task resource ID spec-page https://example.com/spec --kind http
aiculator task fetch ID spec-page

Links are treated as untrusted

A link can come from a ticket that anyone could have edited, so the server refuses to connect to private, loopback or cloud metadata addresses. It checks at connect time, after DNS, and that includes redirects. Only http and https are accepted.

docs.title: From an agent
docs.text:
Agents read this data over MCP, with task_meta and fetch_resource. Small files come back in the answer, and larger ones through GET /v1/blobs/{sha256}.

Agents can read but not write. Writing needs an admin or planner token.

Route Who What GET /v1/tasks/{id}/meta Any token Read properties POST /v1/tasks/{id}/meta Admin, planner Change properties, with null removing one POST /v1/blobs?name= Admin, planner Store bytes GET /v1/blobs/{sha256} Any token Read bytes, always served as a download POST /v1/tasks/{id}/resources/{name} Any token Fetch a foreign resource once POST /v1/tasks/{id}/amend Admin Change what a task says GET /v1/tasks/{id}/priority Admin Explain a priority

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Blobs are not deleted when their task is. A hash can be shared by many tasks, and no cleanup exists yet, so the blob store only grows.

docs.title: Template demo
docs.text:
One template that uses every template feature, in a realistic workflow: shipping a feature, from choosing an approach to opening the pull request.

Source: .agent/template/demo.mdx

Always current: both the source and the output below are included from the real files, and a test fails if a new component is not used in the demo.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
aiculator template --render demo                 # (1)!
aiculator template --render demo --for claude    # (2)!
aiculator template --render demo --set retries=5 # (3)!
aiculator template --install demo                # (4)!
  1. Prints the skill and writes nothing.
  2. Shows what one harness's own copy looks like, naming its real question tool.
  3. Overrides a default from the template's vars.
  4. Writes it to .agents/skills/demo, and links it to each installed harness that needs a link.

Run this from a checkout of this repository

demo.mdx lives in this repository's .agent/template, so it is not bundled in the binary. To use it elsewhere, copy the .agent/template directory into your project.
